source.title: Grokking as Compression: A Nonlinear Complexity Perspective
source.authors: Zi-Ming Liu; Ziqian Zhong; Max Tegmark

record.tranche_reason: The study measures grokking dynamics on algorithmic tasks using linear mapping number (LMN), a different measure from the original studies, and reports its relation to generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own accuracy and complexity results in Section 3 and Figure 2. It also discusses other explanations of grokking, but results cited from those works are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains small networks on three algorithmic tasks and reports delayed generalization (Figure 2). It also proposes a new continuous complexity measure, LMN, which falls steadily between memorization and generalization. This bears on V1 and on V2's claim that continuous progress measures anticipate the jump.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors attribute grokking to compression and say LMN decreases between memorization and generalization. They report that LMN relates linearly to test loss, while L2 relates nonlinearly. They attribute the XOR post-grokking LMN double descent to switching between two nearly degenerate generalizing solutions. They also propose LMN as a neural-network analogue of Kolmogorov complexity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains three-layer SiLU networks on modular addition, S4 permutation composition, and 5-digit XOR with an 80-20 split, and analyzes them using LMN. It does not report an explicit replication of the original recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: For modular addition, the appendix reports that the first hidden layer's LMN is sensitive to hidden progress, while embedding-layer and second-hidden-layer LMN are less meaningful; the second hidden layer largely synchronizes with the training curve.

fits_no_version.finding: On 5-digit XOR, LMN rises briefly after generalization and then falls again. The turning points are about 15 and 20 mappings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: After grokking, networks can switch between nearly degenerate generalizing solutions, visible as a double-descent-like pattern in complexity.

record.problems: Accuracy and LMN trends are mainly presented in plots and qualitative descriptions, without reported uncertainty estimates or repeated-run counts. The study uses one stated 80-20 split and one optimizer/weight-decay setting, and does not vary training-set size.

untested.parts: Whether test accuracy stays at chance during the delay; whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. Only one 80-20 split is used.
Identification of a generalizing circuit (e.g. Fourier algorithm) and the later removal of memorizing components.
Non-algorithmic data; initialization-scale or weight-norm switching.
Weight decay is fixed at 0.2. Critical dataset size and ungrokking are not tested.
Algorithm comparison across runs or architectures.

missing.what: Step counts for memorization (step 200) and generalization (step 7600) on modular addition, quantifying the V1 delay
Layer dependence of LMN: only the first hidden layer tracks hidden progress; embedding and second-layer LMN plateau soon after memorization

record.verdict_notes: This is a short workshop-style preprint with single runs, no uncertainty, and evidence mostly in figures. The sentence comparing LMN and L2 to test loss is garbled in the source. The V2 support covers only the progress-measure part; no circuit is identified. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not report test accuracy remaining at chance during the delay or compare delays across different training-set sizes.
The study measures LMN trends but does not identify a Fourier algorithm, trace a generalizing circuit forming, or show memorizing components being removed.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep is tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
Weight decay is used at one stated value, but the efficiency account, critical dataset size, and ungrokking prediction are not tested.
The study does not compare algorithms across runs.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations.
